Article Title: Since years, OpenAI and Anthropic chased Human Intelligence, and how they may be 'fearing' it now
Article Text:
OpenAI's goal was always AGI. The safety problem came with it

Anthropic built its identity around safer powerful AI

Dario Amodei says AI development may be moving too fast

And then Sam Altman agreed

The race is now about more than human-level intelligence

For the past few years, the race between OpenAI and Anthropic has been about one big idea: building AI systems that can do far more than answer questions, write code or generate images. OpenAI has openly described its mission as ensuring that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, benefits all of humanity. Anthropic, meanwhile, has said that it is preparing for a future with increasingly powerful AI systems that could eventually match or exceed human experts across many fields.Now, the conversation inside both companies is changing.The two AI labs are still building increasingly capable systems. But their leaders are also warning that AI development may be moving so quickly that safety measures could struggle to keep up. Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the industry to slow the pace of AI development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed that frontier AI development needs to be paced and that stronger safety measures are necessary. That creates a striking shift in the AI race. The same companies that spent years trying to make machines more capable are now spending more time asking what happens when those machines become capable enough to act with much greater independence.OpenAI was founded in 2015 with a mission centred on advanced AI. Its stated goal was to develop artificial intelligence in a way that would benefit humanity. The company's later charter defined AGI as highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work.OpenAI has not abandoned that goal. In 2026, it continues to describe AGI as central to its mission. Its current public policy agenda says advanced AI can create risks involving cybersecurity, chemical and biological threats and other areas, while also arguing that AI could bring major economic and social benefits.But OpenAI's own recent research shows why the safety conversation has become harder.This month, the ChatGPT-maker said its upcoming Astra model had reached its "Critical" threshold for cybersecurity capability. OpenAI said that, with the right tools and access, Astra could find previously unknown security flaws and develop ways to exploit them across well-protected systems without a person guiding every step. The company said this required stronger safeguards before deployment.OpenAI has also started talking more openly about unexpected behaviour from its models. The company recently said that it will regularly disclose cases of AI systems showing unexpected or unauthorised behaviour.So the concern is no longer only about an imaginary future where AI becomes smarter than humans. The labs are increasingly dealing with systems that can already act more independently, use tools, operate computers and perform complex tasks.Anthropic, on the other hand, was created with a different emphasis. The company says its mission is to help the world safely transition through transformative AI. Its Claude Constitution says Anthropic believes AI could be one of the most world-changing and potentially dangerous technologies in human history, while also arguing that a safety-focused company should remain at the frontier if powerful AI is coming anyway.That safety focus has produced formal rules around how Anthropic develops increasingly capable models. In 2023, the Claude-maker introduced its Responsible Scaling Policy, designed to address catastrophic risks from increasingly powerful AI systems. It created different safety levels and said stronger safeguards would be required as models crossed specific capability thresholds.Anthropic has since expanded that work. Its current policy says frontier AI could bring major benefits in areas such as science, healthcare and education, but also presents new risks that require safeguards.The company has also created the Anthropic Institute, which it says will study the effects of increasingly powerful AI on society. Anthropic said in March that its models had progressed from early commercial systems to models that could find serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities, perform real-world work and begin accelerating AI development itself.Then came Amodei's latest warning.Earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow down the pace at which frontier models are being improved. His warning came after a series of incidents involving AI agents, including the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident that raised questions about what autonomous AI systems could do when given tools and access.Amodei said:“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”He also warned that the consequences could become much larger as AI systems improve.“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails,”Those are Amodei's projections, not an established prediction about what AI will actually do. But the significance is that the warning is coming from the head of a company actively building frontier AI.Dario Amodei's call for slower development was notable because it came from a direct competitor of OpenAI. But OpenAI CEO Sam Altman soon said he agreed with the central argument.Sam Altman said the frontier needs to be paced and that OpenAI would adopt Amodei's proposal for independent evaluators with employee-like access. A few days later, Altman also described two ways AI progress could go badly: humans losing control of AI and powerful AI becoming concentrated in the hands of one person, company or country.“This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people,” Altman said.That is a notable change in the public conversation.OpenAI is not saying it wants to stop developing more capable AI. Anthropic is not saying it wants to abandon frontier models either. Instead, both are arguing that capability growth and safety work need to move together.There is another reason the language has changed. The target is no longer simply an AI that can answer questions as well as a person. OpenAI says its latest systems can operate computers and graphical interfaces, collaborate with people and other AI systems, and carry out research projects.Anthropic has similarly described the next generation of powerful AI as systems that could navigate digital interfaces, browse the internet, reason through complex tasks for days or weeks and interact with physical equipment. The company has said such systems could emerge as soon as late 2026 or 2027, based on its research trajectory.That is why the debate around AGI is changing. The question is no longer only “Can AI become as intelligent as humans?” It is increasingly “What happens when AI can use that intelligence independently, for long periods, with access to the tools and systems around us?”And that distinction matters.
Article Summary: Anthropic ceo dario amodei called for the industry to slow the pace of ai development. Openai ceo sam altman agreed that frontier ai development needs to be paced and that stronger safety measures are necessary. Dario amodei said we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of ai models.

Article Title: Apple has a new Vision Pro in the works, but a new headset is unlikely before 2028
Article Text:
Apple’s struggles with the Vision Pro

Apple's Vision team is working on the new headset

The pattern of cancelled headsets

What’s Next for Apple

Apple is reportedly developing a new Vision Pro headset, but as per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the project is still in early stages and may not reach consumers until late 2028 or early 2029. The company is said to be working on multiple design concepts, including lighter models and offload computing power to external devices. This is the same approach which Facebook-parent Meta opted for in its recently launched VR Glasses.The Vision Pro, launched in February 2024 at nearly $4,000, has struggled to gain traction. Sales remain sluggish, with some Apple retail stores reporting only a handful of units sold each month. Internally, Apple has shelved several headset prototypes over the past two years, including Vision Air (N100) and N109, both aimed at reducing weight and cost. Leadership changes under new CEO John Ternus have further reshaped the Vision hardware team, signaling skepticism about the product’s long-term viability.Apple's Vision team is working on the new headset under the code name N224. Engineers are exploring about four concepts.Some of them offload internal components to an external unit, the same approach Meta used in its new VR Glasses, which Gurman says weigh one-sixth as much as the Vision Pro at one-third of the price.Not everyone at Apple is on board with that direction. Gurman reports that some senior decision-makers see an external puck as a poor user experience and want Apple to stay closer to an all-in-one design. He describes the work as being on "life support" while the company weighs a new direction, and there is no guarantee the device will ever ship.N224 follows several shelved projects. About two years ago, Apple dropped N107, a design that would have offloaded computing to a Mac or other device to cut the headset's bulk. A year ago it shelved N100, a "Vision Air" that would have moved more components into an external pack. Another project, N109, envisioned as a lighter, cheaper Vision Pro with a less powerful chip, was also cancelled.The Vision Pro launched in February 2024 and has not sold well. Gurman says Apple retail employees report that many stores are lucky to sell one unit a month, and Apple now promotes the roughly $4,000 device for uses such as surgery, effectively positioning it as a specialist product.Apple engineers are now working on a revamped headset under the code name N224, exploring four different concepts. Some designs mimic Meta’s external computing puck, while others stick closer to Apple’s all-in-one philosophy. However, insiders describe the project as being on “life support,” with no guarantee it will ever launch. For now, Apple is focusing on smart glasses and other wearables, including AirPods with camera sensors and a fitness-style band.
Article Summary: The vision pro launched in february 2024 at nearly $4,000. Sales remain sluggish, with some apple retail stores reporting only a handful of units sold each month. Apple engineers are now working on a revamped headset under the code name n224, exploring four different concepts.

Article Title: In the early 1900s, a United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington, D.C.; later promoted for soil protection, the “wonder plant” spread across millions of acres of the South
Article Text:
A United States plant explorer tested Japanese kudzu near Washington. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

David Fairchild

planted kudzu seedlings around his home in 1902

More than 1.2 million acres were planted after the Soil Conservation Service backed kudzu

Kudzu's growth rate rises with carbon dioxide, and it spends little on woody tissue

Kudzu (

Pueraria montana

): History, Physiology, and Ecology Combine to Make a Major Ecosystem Threat

Nitrogen fixation more than doubles

nitric oxide emissions

from invaded soils

Soil erosion, brownout. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Forest Service survey data puts kudzu on about 227,000 acres of Southern forestland

Kudzu was no accident of nature: federal agencies promoted it and paid for it, and the evidence shows an ecological impact that is real but smaller than the legend suggests. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 as a USDA agency and now known as the Natural Resources Conservation Service, tested, praised, and paid farmers to plant kudzu in the 1930s and 1940s, before the ecological cost was counted, as naturalist Bill Finch recounts in Smithsonian Magazine.Kudzu first reached the United States as an ornamental vine in the Japanese pavilion at the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876. A paper from the USDA Forest Service Southern Research Station picks up the story from there. David Fairchild, the plant explorer, had seen farmers in Japan using kudzu for grazing, and in 1902 he planted kudzu seedlings in his garden near Washington, D.C., to see how the plant would behave. By 1907, kudzu hay had been demonstrated in Jamestown, Virginia, a sign of growing interest in the plant as livestock feed. Fairchild, however, grew wary of it. By 1938, he had turned against the plant, and in his autobiography, The World Was My Garden, he recalled firsthand how kudzu covered bushes and climbed pines, smothering them. That account reflects Fairchild's own experience with his experiment, not an official USDA position on kudzu.C. E. Pleas, a farmer from Chipley, Florida, discovered that livestock eagerly ate kudzu. After confirming with the USDA that the plant was not poisonous, he promoted it as a forage crop through newspaper articles and pamphlets, according to Florida Memory, the Florida Department of State's archive program. He turned into an avid fan of the crop and planted 35 acres to sell as fodder. In the 1930s and 1940s, the Soil Conservation Service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the South, particularly in the Piedmont regions of Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi. The agency distributed more than 85 million seedlings and paid farmers to plant the vine. The farmers were paid to plant kudzu, and more than 1.2 million acres were planted under this federal program. This number covers only the acreage planted under the federal program, not all the kudzu planted in the U.S., and Bill Finch's reporting in Smithsonian Magazine puts total plantings at a little more than a million acres by 1945.Why did the vine take so well?, published in Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences in 2004, offers part of the answer. The growth of kudzu is stimulated significantly by increased levels of CO₂, according to Irwin Forseth and Anne Innis of the University of Maryland, College Park. Because kudzu does not invest in woody structure, this growth boost could make it even more competitive as atmospheric CO₂ concentrations rise. A fast-growing plant that invests little in woody tissue can outcompete slower-growing rivals.The plant also alters the soil it grows in. Jonathan Hickman and colleagues showed this in "Kudzu (Pueraria montana) Invasion Doubles Emissions of Nitric Oxide and Increases Ozone Pollution," published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2010. The authors point to the southeastern United States as an area of particular concern: because kudzu fixes nitrogen, it drives extra nitric oxide emissions from the soil, and nitric oxide feeds ozone formation. In 2007, the team studied soils at three sites in Madison County, Georgia. In invaded soils, net nitrogen mineralization rose by up to 1,000% and net nitrification by up to 500% compared with control soils, and nitric oxide emissions were more than 100% higher (2.81 versus 1.24 ng NO‑N cm⁻² h⁻¹). Only these figures are field measurements.The researchers then fed their data into the GEOS‑Chem atmospheric chemistry model and assumed an extreme scenario in which kudzu invaded all nonagricultural, nonurban soils across nine southeastern states. Under that scenario, soil nitric oxide emissions rose by 28%, and some areas saw up to seven additional days each summer when 8-hour ozone concentrations exceeded 70 ppb. These are projections, not measurements.Kudzu is often said to cover seven million to nine million acres of the United States, but Bill Finch, writing in Smithsonian Magazine's "The True Story of Kudzu, the Vine That Never Truly Ate the South," reports that scientists reassessing its spread found nothing close to that. Forest Service survey data from 2010 shows that 227,000 acres of southern forestland contain kudzu, about one-tenth of 1 percent of the region's 200 million acres of forestland. This estimate covers forestland only, so kudzu growing on other land is not counted.The Forest Service expects the infested forestland to grow by no more than 2,500 acres a year, while some sources repeat an unsupported figure of 150,000 acres a year. The research on kudzu's ecology helps explain why the plant competes so well. Forseth and Innis (2004) attribute kudzu's edge to two physiological traits: a fast response to high CO₂ concentrations and little investment in woody tissue. Much of what people say about kudzu's ecological effects comes from testimony rather than measurement, which is why the Forest Service survey and the studies above matter. It was planted deliberately, its growth habits give it a competitive edge, and its effects on soil chemistry reach as far as the air above it. Its environmental impact is smaller than some legends suggest.
Article Summary: Kudzu first reached the united states as an ornamental vine in the japanese pavilion at the philadelphia centennial exposition of 1876. In the 1930s and 1940s, the soil conservation service promoted kudzu as a means of stabilizing soil in the rapidly eroded gullies of the south.

Article Title: California thieves steal Nvidia-branded trailers expecting expensive AI hardware; find 40,000 pounds of sand instead
Article Text:
California thieves found sand inside the Nvidia-branded trailers

What was inside the stolen trailers

Why PlusAI uses sand to test autonomous trucks

How the stolen trailers were found

What police said about the theft

The connection between PlusAI and Nvidia

Two Nvidia-branded trailers belonging to autonomous-trucking company PlusAI were stolen from outside its warehouse in Fremont, California, on September 23, 2026. The trailers were associated with PlusAI's work with Nvidia on autonomous-driving technology, but instead of carrying GPUs, servers or other expensive AI equipment, each contained about 20,000 pounds of sand. The pair therefore carried roughly 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons, of sand. PlusAI uses the material as simulated cargo during autonomous-truck testing to reproduce the weight of real freight. The trailers were later discovered in nearby Newark after an acquaintance of a PlusAI executive spotted them, while police continued investigating the theft.The two trailers were parked outside PlusAI's Fremont facility when they were taken overnight. Their locks were broken and the thieves apparently arrived with tractor units, connected them to the trailers and drove away. Both trailers prominently displayed PlusAI and Nvidia branding, reflecting the companies' work in autonomous trucking and artificial intelligence.The company's autonomous-driving truck cabs remained inside the facility and were not stolen. The stolen trailers were later located in Newark, California, roughly half a mile from PlusAI's Fremont warehouse.The trailers contained about 20,000 pounds of sand each, giving them a combined load of approximately 40,000 pounds, or 20 tons. The sand was being used as simulated cargo during PlusAI's testing programme.Heavy simulated cargo allows autonomous-truck developers to reproduce the conditions of a loaded commercial vehicle without using an actual freight shipment. The added weight can be used to test how a truck responds during acceleration, braking, turning and other driving conditions.PlusAI develops autonomous-driving technology for commercial trucks, meaning its vehicles must be tested under conditions that resemble real-world freight operations. Vehicle behaviour can change significantly depending on how much weight a truck is carrying.Using sand provides a practical way to create a controlled and consistent load. Engineers can adjust the amount of weight while testing different driving scenarios, helping them study how the autonomous system and vehicle respond when operating under the demands of a loaded truck.The trailers were eventually spotted in Newark, close to PlusAI's Fremont facility. An acquaintance of a PlusAI executive reportedly noticed the trailers and sent a photograph to the executive after recognising them.The company contacted authorities, who located and recovered both trailers. The sand was still inside, allowing PlusAI to recover both the vehicles and their testing cargo.The Fremont Police Department investigated the theft after the trailers were reported missing. Security footage reportedly showed two unidentified tractor units near the PlusAI facility around the time of the incident.PlusAI said the tractor units did not belong to the company. Investigators were working to identify the people involved and determine how the trailers were taken from the facility.The Nvidia branding on the trailers reflected the companies' collaboration in autonomous trucking. PlusAI works with Nvidia on computing and artificial-intelligence technology used in autonomous vehicles.Nvidia's technology is widely used in AI development and autonomous-driving systems, making its branding highly recognisable in the technology industry. However, the trailers themselves were being used by PlusAI for autonomous-truck testing, with the confirmed cargo consisting of sand rather than Nvidia computing equipment.The theft produced an unexpected discovery when two trailers carrying prominent technology-company branding turned out to be loaded with 40,000 pounds of sand. The trailers had been taken from PlusAI's Fremont facility but were found only about half a mile away in Newark.Both trailers and their simulated cargo were recovered, while investigators continued working to identify the people responsible for the theft.
Article Summary: California thieves found sand inside the nvidia-branded trailers. Plusai uses the material as simulated cargo during autonomous-truck testing to reproduce the weight of real freight. The trailers contained about 20,000 pounds of sand each, giving them a combined load of approximately 40,000lbs, or 20 tons.

Article Title: Pakistan goes bananas over giant gorillas dancing to Bollywood songs
Article Text:
Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online (Photo: AFP)

Pakistanis are going bananas over a trend that has crossed the Indian border: Giant gorillas, dancing to Bollywood music.Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online, turning them into the surprise stars of weddings, birthdays and other festivities.In the videos, guests can be seen joining in alongside the costumed entertainers, many of them visibly delighted by the unusual addition to their celebrations. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding DJ tracks while partygoers gather round and dance, creating a lively, comic spectacle that has quickly drawn attention across social media.Behind the trend in Lahore is Shayen Zahoor, who runs Gorilla.co.pk, a business offering giant dancing gorilla acts for events across the city.Speaking to AFP, Zahoor explained how quickly the idea took off. He said the costume was ordered in early April and arrived by the end of the same month, after which the team wasted no time putting it to use.Once the suit arrived, he and his team lost no time getting started."We uploaded a reel on Instagram, and within just two days it reached a million views," Zahoor recalled.The overwhelming response convinced them to treat the venture as a serious business, and bookings soon began pouring in, with the public reaction proving remarkably enthusiastic."On the very first day, we received approximately 1,200 to 1,300 messages," he said, describing how curious would-be customers flooded his inbox.Many wanted to know whether the costume had genuinely arrived, what it would cost to book, and other practical details before making up their minds.What began as a single Instagram reel has since snowballed into a full-fledged entertainment phenomenon, with giant gorillas now a familiar, if unlikely, fixture at Pakistani celebrations.
Article Summary: Pakistanis are going bananas over a trend that has crossed the indian border: giant gorillas, dancing to bollywood music. Clips of these larger-than-life performers have been spreading rapidly online. The performers swing their oversized arms to pounding dj tracks while partygoers gather round and dance.
